historical_record.description: The Board of Permit Appeals upheld the revocation of a demolition permit for the building at 236 Monterey Boulevard.
The City Planning Commission unanimously refused to reclassify the lot from RH-2 to RM-1 (Resolution 8162).
The Merrill Conservatory here was partly demolished under a demolition permit issued in error, until the Planning Commission barred further demolition.
The Park and Recreation and Planning Commissions jointly recommended that the city acquire the partly demolished conservatory, through the Trust for Public Land.

William Augustus Merralls, a mining engineer and inventor, bought the seven-lot property and had the conservatory built. No record gives the date of building; the structure alone cost $7,000, and most of the trees and plants on the grounds eight decades later were those he planted.

Ernest Van Beck and his wife bought the property from the bank for $12,000, taking the house for the only building on it; they came on the overgrown conservatory by accident and had the grounds cleared and restored.
The conservatory was given landmark status on September 21, 1975, through the efforts of the Sunnyside Neighborhood Association.
Merralls was killed by a train on September 1, 1914, his fortune tied up in an aircraft company and the property heavily mortgaged; his widow let the bank foreclose two years later.
The conservatory's official dedication was held at a Sunday in the Park, with a chorus, cloggers and a display of 150 historical photographs.
